title: Capstone: A Concurrent URL Health Checker

questions.prompt: Why use a bounded worker pool instead of one goroutine per URL?

options.text: To cap concurrency and resource use for large inputs

questions.explanation: With thousands of URLs, one goroutine each could exhaust memory or file descriptors; a fixed pool keeps resource use predictable.

questions.prompt: In the worker pool, who closes `jobs` and who closes `results`?

options.text: The producer closes jobs; a goroutine closes results after wg.Wait()
The workers close jobs; main closes results first
Both are closed by the receiver

questions.explanation: The producer closes jobs after sending all URLs; results is closed once wg.Wait() confirms all workers finished, so each range ends cleanly.

questions.prompt: Why does the program sort results before printing them?

options.text: Because workers finish in nondeterministic order; sorting makes output stable and testable

questions.explanation: Concurrent completion order is nondeterministic; sorting by URL yields deterministic, testable output.

questions.prompt: The program calls os.____(1) when any check fails so scripts and CI can detect failure.
questions.explanation: A non-zero exit code (os.Exit(1)) lets automation branch on failure without parsing the text output.

questions.prompt: How do you test HTTP client code without hitting the real network?

options.text: Use net/http/httptest.NewServer and point the client at it
Hardcode expected responses in the client

questions.explanation: httptest.NewServer runs a local test server; srv.Client()/srv.URL let you exercise success, error-status, and failure paths reliably.

questions.prompt: Match each earlier concept to how the capstone uses it.

pairs.right: Bound each request and allow cancellation
Configure workers and timeout from the CLI

questions.explanation: The capstone combines context timeouts, a channel/WaitGroup worker pool, disciplined body closing, and flag-based configuration.
